questions.q: After tsc removes the types, what does const task = raw as Task; become?
questions.explain: A type assertion is erased completely: no check, no conversion. That is type erasure. as only changes what the compiler believes about the value.
options: const task = raw instanceof Task ? raw : null;

questions.q: Which part of function label(task: Task, status: Status = "todo"): string is still there when Node.js runs the code?
questions.explain: A default value is plain JavaScript, so it stays: the compiled line is function label(task, status = "todo"). Annotations, interfaces and type aliases are removed.

questions.q: Which of these still does something when the program runs?
questions.explain: typeof, in, instanceof, Array.isArray, #private and Object.freeze are real JavaScript. readonly, as, private and import type exist only at compile time.

questions.q: Task is an interface. What does tsc say about return value instanceof Task;?
questions.explain: An interface does not exist at runtime, so there is nothing to compare with (TS2693). instanceof works with classes, because a class is also a real JavaScript value. For an interface, check its parts with typeof, in and Array.isArray.
options: Nothing: it checks whether the value has all the fields of Task
An error: Task only refers to a type, but is used as a value here
An error: instanceof is not allowed in TypeScript

questions.q: Why does const task: Task = JSON.parse(requestBody); compile even when the body is {"title": 42}?
questions.explain: The JSON arrives while the program runs; the compiler never saw it. any switches checking off, so the type annotation is a promise nobody checks. Type the result as unknown and validate it.
options: Because TypeScript checks the JSON when the program starts
Because JSON.parse returns any, and the compiler believes whatever type you give it
Because Task is an interface, and interfaces accept anything
It does not compile; tsc reads the JSON string and reports the error

questions.q: Which of these values was never seen by the compiler, and must be checked at runtime?
questions.explain: Request bodies, query strings, environment variables, files, database rows and other APIs all arrive as text while the program runs, possibly from an attacker. Values you create in your own code are followed by the compiler.
options: A constant you wrote in the same file
The return value of a function you wrote that returns number
The body of an HTTP request sent to your API
An object literal you pass to a typed function

questions.q: What does the type assertion body as NewTask do?
questions.explain: as means "trust me". It compiles to nothing, so a wrong value stays wrong and fails later. On outside data, as is never a check.
options: It checks the fields and throws if one is wrong
It converts the fields to the right types
It changes the type the compiler believes, and never the value
It removes fields that are not in NewTask

questions.q: Which use of as does the lesson call always safe?
questions.explain: as const makes a type narrower (readonly literal types), not different, so it cannot lie. The others claim outside data or a string is something it is not.

questions.q: What does the ! in users.get(id)!.email do?
questions.explain: Like as and any, ! switches the compiler off for one spot. If the user is missing, the program crashes when reading .email. Prefer a real check.
options: It checks at runtime that the user exists and throws a clear error if not
It tells the compiler "this is not null or undefined, trust me", with no runtime check
It turns undefined into an empty object

questions.q: What does the return type value is NewTask tell TypeScript?
questions.explain: This is a type predicate. The function returns a boolean, and inside if (isNewTask(body)) TypeScript narrows body to NewTask.
options: That the function converts value into a NewTask
That when the function returns true, the argument is a NewTask
That the function throws if value is not a NewTask

questions.q: A type guard declares value is User but its body only checks that email exists. What does tsc do?
questions.explain: TypeScript does not compare a guard's body with its value is T promise. Guards are the one place where a type can lie, so keep them short and write tests for them.
options: It reports that the guard does not check every field of User
Nothing: it believes the predicate, so the bug only shows up at runtime
It adds the missing checks automatically
It narrows only to { email: unknown }

questions.q: When should you use an assertion function (asserts value is T) instead of a type guard (value is T)?
questions.explain: A type guard returns a boolean and you write the if. An assertion function throws on bad data; when it returns normally, the value has the checked type on every following line.
options: When bad data should stop the work: it throws, and after it returns the value is narrowed for the rest of the code
When you want to choose what to do with bad data in an if
When the value comes from your own code
Never: assertion functions are erased at runtime

questions.q: With strict on, why is console.log(error.message) inside catch (error) an error?
questions.explain: throw "a plain string" is legal, and a string has no message. So error is unknown (TS18046). Check it with error instanceof Error first. Never write catch (error: any): it only hides the question.
options: Because JavaScript can throw anything, not only Error objects, so error is unknown

questions.q: A client sends {"title": "Fix bug", "id": 999, "role": "admin"} to create a task. What is the safe way to build the new task?
questions.explain: Allow-list the fields. Spreading or asserting keeps whatever the client added, which is the mass assignment hole. Deleting known-bad fields misses the next one someone invents.
options: body as NewTask, because NewTask has no role field
Copy only the allowed, checked fields: { title, done, priority }
Delete id and role from body, then spread the rest

questions.q: Where should raw request data be validated?
questions.explain: Validate once at the boundary. Inner functions like createTask(input: NewTask) take only checked types, so the compiler guarantees they never see unchecked data and never need to check again.
options: In every function that uses the data, just to be safe
Once, at the edge (the handler), turning unknown into a precise type that inner functions accept
Nowhere, if the types are correct
In the database, when the row is saved

questions.q: The create-task handler answers three cases. Which set of status codes does the lesson use?
questions.explain: Text that is not JSON at all is a bad request (400). Valid JSON with wrong fields is 422 with the list of issues. A new task is 201 Created.

questions.q: What type does process.env.PORT have?
questions.explain: Environment variables are always strings, or missing. That is why readPort takes string | undefined and converts and checks the value itself.

questions.q: In parseNewTask, the last if repeats typeof done !== "boolean" even though issues already records it. Why?
questions.explain: Narrowing follows the checks the compiler can see. An empty issues array says nothing about the type of done, so without the repeated check, done would still be unknown in the returned object.
options: To check the value twice, in case it changed
The compiler cannot connect "the array is empty" to "these checks passed", so the checks are written where it can see them
It is a mistake; the line can be removed without any error

questions.q: What is the main risk of a hand-written validator next to a separate NewTask interface?
questions.explain: The type and the check are written twice and can drift apart. @zudojs/schema describes the shape once and gives you the type with Infer, so they can never disagree.
options: Someone adds a field to the interface and forgets the validator, and nothing warns them

questions.explain: The annotation Task is erased, and JSON.parse returns any, so nothing checks the data. The types said string and boolean; the data said number and string, and the data won.
options: TypeError: title must be a string

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: TypeError is a subclass of Error, so instanceof Error is true and its message is used. Anything else is turned into a string with String(), so 404 becomes '404'.

questions.q: Task is a class this time. What does this print?
questions.explain: A class is a real value, so instanceof works. But JSON only ever produces plain objects and arrays. Even with the same fields, the parsed object was not made by new Task, so it is not a Task instance.
options: TypeError: Right-hand side of 'instanceof' is not callable

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: in only asks whether the property exists; a value of null still counts. So you must also check the property's type. And typeof null is "object".

questions.explain: ! only silences the compiler. get still returns undefined for a missing key, and the crash comes one line later. A real check like if (price === undefined) would have caught it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The result is built from named, checked fields only, so id and role are dropped and the title is trimmed. The validator collects every issue instead of stopping at the first one.

questions.q: A validator reads const done = input.done ?? false;. What does this print?
questions.explain: ?? uses the default only for undefined and null. 0 is kept, which is right: it is not a boolean, so the next check reports "done must be true or false" instead of silently changing it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing value gets the default. 80.5 is not a whole number and 70000 is above 65535, so both are errors. Checking result.ok narrows the union, so value and error are each allowed on their side.
options:
bad PORT "undefined"
8080
bad PORT "80.5"
bad PORT "70000"

questions.q: This guard compiles. What does the program print?
questions.explain: The guard only checks that email exists, so it returns true, and TypeScript believes the body is a User. But tags is missing. tsc never compares a guard's body with its value is User promise.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'join')
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'tags')

questions.q: Write the type guard isRecord(value): it returns true only for a plain object, not for null, not for an array, and not for other values. The program should print [ true, false, false, false ].
questions.explain: typeof value === "object" is also true for null and arrays, so each needs its own test. With value is Record<string, unknown>, every property is still unknown and must be checked before use.

questions.q:
Write the type guard isProduct(value). A Product is an object with a string name and a number price. The program should print:

MILK 1.2
invalid
invalid
questions.explain: Check every field the type promises, with its real type: "2" is a string, so the second body is refused. After "name" in value, TypeScript lets you read value.name as unknown, and typeof narrows it.

questions.q:
Write the assertion function assertTitle(value). It throws a TypeError with the message title must be a non-empty string unless value is a string with at least one non-space character. After the call, value is a string. The program should print:

BUY MILK
TypeError: title must be a non-empty string
TypeError: title must be a non-empty string
questions.explain: An assertion function returns nothing when the value is fine and throws otherwise. Because its return type is asserts value is string, input.toUpperCase() is allowed on the next line.

BUY MILK
TypeError: title must be a non-empty string
TypeError: title must be a non-empty string

questions.q:
Write messageOf(error: unknown): return the message when error is an Error, otherwise String(error). The program should print:

bad JSON: something broke
thrown: a plain string
questions.explain: In catch, the error is unknown because anything can be thrown. instanceof Error is a runtime check (Error is a class), so it narrows and .message is allowed.
questions.expected:
bad JSON: something broke
thrown: a plain string

questions.q:
Write readPort(value: string | undefined) for process.env.PORT. Missing or empty means 3000. A whole number from 1 to 65535 is returned as a number. Anything else is an error with the message PORT must be 1 to 65535. The program should print:

{"ok":true,"value":3000}
{"ok":true,"value":8080}
{"ok":false,"error":"PORT must be 1 to 65535"}
{"ok":false,"error":"PORT must be 1 to 65535"}
questions.explain: Environment variables are strings or missing, so convert and check them yourself. Number("http") is NaN, which is not an integer. Returning a Result makes the caller handle the bad case.

questions.q:
This guard only checks that email exists. Fix it so it also checks that email is a string and that tags is an array of strings. The program should print:

not a user
not a user
ada@example.com: admin, dev
questions.explain: A guard must check every field its predicate promises, including the items inside arrays. tsc will not tell you when a check is missing, because it simply believes value is User.
questions.expected:
not a user
not a user

questions.q:
Write parseSignup(body: unknown). It returns { email, name } with both trimmed, built from those two fields only, so extra fields like role are dropped. If body is not an object, or either field is not a non-empty string, return null. The program should print:

{"email":"ada@example.com","name":"Ada"}
null
questions.explain: The returned object is built from two checked variables, so nothing else the client sent can get through. Spreading body would have let "role": "admin" in: the mass assignment hole.

questions.q:
Write taskIssues(body), which returns every problem, not just the first. body is already known to be an object. Add title must be 3 to 100 characters when title (trimmed) is not a string of that length, and done must be true or false when done is present but not a boolean. The program should print:

[]
[ 'title must be 3 to 100 characters', 'done must be true or false' ]
[ 'title must be 3 to 100 characters' ]
questions.explain: Push each problem into an array instead of returning early, so the client can fix everything in one go. A title that is not a string counts as "", which fails the length check.
questions.expected:
[]
[ 'title must be 3 to 100 characters', 'done must be true or false' ]
[ 'title must be 3 to 100 characters' ]

questions.q: Finish handle(rawBody). If JSON.parse throws, return status 400. If the parsed body is not an object with a string title, return 422. Otherwise return 201. The program should print [ 400, 422, 422, 201 ].
questions.explain: Declare body as unknown so the any from JSON.parse cannot spread. Broken JSON is a bad request (400); valid JSON with the wrong shape is 422.

questions.q:
Write the type guard isStringArray(value): true only for an array whose items are all strings. The program should print:

a+b
not a string array
not a string array
questions.explain: Array.isArray is a runtime check that also narrows. Then every item must be checked too: an array of unknown is not an array of strings until you have looked at each one.
questions.expected:
a+b
not a string array
not a string array

questions.q: Write the type guard isPriority(value) using the PRIORITIES list, then readPriority(value): undefined gives "normal", a valid priority is returned, and anything else gives null. The program should print [ 'normal', 'high', null, null ].
questions.explain: PRIORITIES is a real value, so it can be used at runtime; the Priority type cannot. some((p) => p === value) works for any unknown value, while includes would need an as.
